## IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.

### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. **Fiscal Impact:** Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. YES A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: The state would *not* collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

PRO Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. CON Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. ## PROP

## IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***California Is Home to Many Billionaires.*** Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.

***Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending.*** The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.

### PROPOSAL

***Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires.*** Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.

***Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care.*** The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax.*** The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.

***Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues.*** California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.

***State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax.*** The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

### ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 40

YES ON PROP. 40 TO TAX BILLIONAIRES

Trump’s “Big, Ugly Bill” slashed funding for healthcare in California to pay for more billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. Vote YES on Prop. 40 to make billionaires finally pay their fair share in taxes and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.

FUND HEALTHCARE, NOT BILLIONAIRE TAX BREAKS

Prop. 40 makes approximately 200 California billionaires pay a modest, one-time tax on their global wealth to keep local hospitals and ERs open and healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.

It will raise about $100 billion to replace the funding Trump and his billionaire donors took from working people to line their pockets. The funds will go to life-saving medical care for seniors, veterans, and families. It will allow millions of Californians to keep their health insurance and not see their premiums skyrocket. It will prevent mass teacher layoffs in our public schools and keep children fed through food assistance programs.

BILLIONAIRES SHOULD PAY THEIR FAIR SHARE

You pay your taxes out of every paycheck, but billionaires pay much lower rates than working families. They insist on paying less, even as they get bigger and bigger tax breaks.

Prop. 40 enacts a one-time tax paid ONLY by Californians worth more than $1 billion, a small group of people who together hold $2 trillion in wealth—most of which will never be taxed due to loopholes that favor the ultra-wealthy.

# **Proposition 40**

Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.

* * *

## Analysis of Measure

### Background

***California Is Home to Many Billionaires.*** Several of the wealthiest people in the world live in California. Wealth is the value of all the things a person owns. Wealth is different from income, which is how much a person earns in a set period of time, like one year. A person’s wealth typically is measured by their net worth. A person’s net worth is the value of all the things they own, like stocks, businesses, or other investments, minus their debts. California is home to a few hundred people with net worth over $1 billion, often called billionaires. Many of these billionaires gained their wealth as executives or investors in California technology companies.

***Health Care Is a Major Category of State Spending.*** The state and federal government spend over $200 billion per year on state health care programs. Most state health care spending is for Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income people. State spending also supports public health programs, mental health care, and drug and alcohol treatment.

### Proposal

***Establishes One-Time Wealth Tax on Billionaires.*** Under Proposition 40, billionaires who were residents of California on January 1, 2026 would have to pay a one-time state tax equal to 5 percent of their net worth. The tax would be due in 2027. Taxpayers would have the option to spread the payments over five years but would have to pay more to do so. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.

***Most of the Money Must Be Spent on Health Care.*** The state would decide how and when to spend the money from the wealth tax, but it would have to be spent on certain types of services. Ninety percent of the money would have to be spent on health care services for the public. The rest would have to be spent on education, food assistance, and administration of the wealth tax. Existing rules in the State Constitution that limit spending and require the state to spend a certain amount on schools and community colleges would not apply to this money.

#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions

If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more “yes” votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 41 or 42 conflict with Proposition 40.

### Fiscal Effects

***Temporary State Revenue Increase From Wealth Tax.*** The state probably would collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax. This temporary increase in state tax collections would be spread across several years. Exactly when and how much the state would collect is very hard to predict for many reasons. For example, it is hard to know what actions billionaires would take to reduce the amount of tax they pay. Also, much of the wealth is based on stock prices, which are always changing.

***Possible Ongoing Decrease in State Income Tax Revenues.*** California billionaires, like all those earning money in the state, currently pay state taxes on their annual income. Billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away. These responses probably would reduce state revenues by less than $1 billion per year. This could mean less money for the state’s General Fund, which is the account that pays for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.

***State Costs to Administer the Wealth Tax.*** The state would have costs to determine how much wealth tax is owed and to collect tax payments. These costs could be tens of millions of dollars per year for several years. These costs would be paid from the new wealth tax revenues.

* * *

## Yes/No Statement

A **YES** vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

A **NO** vote on this measure means: The state would *not* collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

* * *

## Summary of Legislative Analyst’s Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact

*   Temporary state revenue increase from a new wealth tax on billionaires. These wealth tax revenues probably would add up to tens of billions of dollars spread over several years.
*   Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in state income tax revenue collected from billionaires.

* * *

## Ballot Label

**Fiscal Impact**: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires.

The measure originated as Initiative 25-0024 (filed October 2025, amended November 2025), qualified in June 2026, and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW. It faces competing “poison pill” measures (Props 41 and 42) that could prevent it from taking effect if they receive more yes votes, even if Prop 40 also passes a majority. Legal challenges are widely expected (retroactivity, Commerce Clause apportionment of worldwide assets, due process, etc.), with the measure including expedited review, severability, and instructions for courts to reform dates if needed to preserve the tax.[[2]](https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/)

### Text Highlights (Constitutional Amendment and Statute)
The constitutional change adds Article XIII, Section 37, specifically authorizing “a one-time tax on the accumulated wealth of California billionaires” (residents as of the tax obligation date of January 1, 2026, per existing residency rules). It explicitly allows taxation of all forms of personal property/wealth (tangible or intangible) for this purpose, overrides conflicting constitutional provisions for this revenue, and creates a dedicated reserve fund with spending rules and caps (e.g., up to $22.5 billion/year for health). The statutory portion (new Revenue and Taxation Code Part 27, §§ 50300 et seq.) details the tax as an “excise tax” on “the activity of sustaining excessive accumulations of wealth,” valuation rules, pull-backs, administration, and more. Full text is available via the Attorney General (Initiative 25-0024A1, ~32 pages) and voter guide.[[3]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

Key anti-avoidance and counting rules include:
- Gifts over $1 million after October 15, 2025, and transfers to non-grantor trusts (full for 2026, 75% for 2025) are generally pulled back into the giver’s net worth.
- Related-party or non-arm’s-length debts do not reduce net worth; charitable pledges after October 15, 2025, generally do not.
- Temporary relocation of tangible personal property to avoid tax is disallowed.
- A general anti-avoidance rule allows the Franchise Tax Board to recast transactions lacking economic substance or whose substantial purpose was an unintended tax benefit.
- Applicable trusts can be taxed separately.[[4]](https://ridleylawoffices.com/california-billionaire-tax-prop-40/)

Section 50310 of the proposed statute states: “The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” This is a relatively common clause in California initiatives. The constitutional authorization itself is narrowly framed around a *one-time* tax on *billionaires* as of the specified dates.[[3]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

### Loophole/Amendment Analysis
Opponents (including some ads and groups) have argued this creates a “Trojan horse” or loophole allowing the Legislature (with a future governor) to expand the tax—e.g., lower the $1 billion threshold, raise the rate, make it recurring, or apply it more broadly—via a two-thirds vote, potentially without returning to voters. They note California’s history of extending “temporary” taxes (e.g., Prop 30/55). Hoover Institution analysis highlights that the threshold, rate, and “one-time” nature could theoretically be changed.[[5]](https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40)

Fact-checks and legal experts describe this as only *partially* true, with important limits:
- Amendments must be “consistent with and further the purposes” of the Act (protecting health care/education/food via a narrowly applicable one-time billionaire wealth tax). California courts give the Legislature latitude (“by any reasonable construction”), as in past cases like Prop 57 amendments, but it is not unlimited.
- Expanding to non-billionaires, making it ongoing, or fundamentally altering the one-time/billionaire focus would likely conflict with the constitutional language (which voters would have approved) and the stated purposes. Changing the Constitution itself generally requires another ballot measure.
- The measure writes the core authorization into the Constitution, not just statute. Opponents’ claims often omit this.
- Practical/political hurdles exist: two-thirds is a high bar, and any expansion would face litigation, voter backlash, and billionaire flight risks (already observed pre-election).
- The Legislature *could* tweak administrative details (valuation methods, exclusions, reporting, spending timing within caps) more readily if they further the purposes. It could also abolish the reserve fund once revenues are collected/spent.[[6]](https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/)

- **Valuation disputes**: Private assets start with a formula that may overstate value; taxpayers can submit appraisals but face a high “clear and convincing” bar.

- **Implementation/administration**: New valuation system for art, IP, private businesses, etc., within six months; high litigation risk; all filers must report.
- **Behavioral responses**: Possible income tax revenue loss (<$1 billion/year ongoing per LAO) from departures or income shifting; revenue highly sensitive to asset values and avoidance.
- **Spending**: Legislature has discretion on timing/amounts (within earmarks and “not to supplant” rules), and funds are not strictly tied to offsetting specific federal cuts.

Proponents emphasize the narrow, one-time design, anti-avoidance rules, and emergency health care purpose (tied to projected federal Medi-Cal cuts). ## Overview

### What would the initiative do?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design) and [2026 competing California tax measures](#2026_competing_California_tax_measures)*

The initiative would enact a one-time tax of 5% on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest. The tax would be retroactive and apply to taxpayers residing in the state as of January 1, 2026. The tax would be due with an individual's 2027 tax filings. The initiative would allow individuals to pay the tax in five equal installments beginning in 2027, with each subsequent payment subject to an annual deferral charge of 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

The initiative would create the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, where all taxes, interest, and penalties resulting from the initiative would be deposited. The fund would have two sub-accounts: the Billionaire Tax Health account, where 90% of the revenue would be deposited, and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account with the remaining 10% of revenue. The initiative would fund Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low- and moderate-income individuals; health care access, benefits, and services; public education from K-14; and food assistance programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood, or California's Universal Meals Program for school meals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

Two measures — [Proposition 41, the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative](/California_Proposition_41,_Prohibit_Excluding_New_State_Taxes_from_Spending_Limit_and_Require_Special_Tax_Audits_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 41, Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative (2026)") and [Proposition 42, the Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings Initiative](/California_Proposition_42,_Prohibit_New_Taxes_on_Retirement_Holdings,_Personal_Assets,_and_Savings_and_Limit_Retroactive_Taxes_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Proposition 42, Prohibit New Taxes on Retirement Holdings, Personal Assets, and Savings and Limit Retroactive Taxes Initiative (2026)") — are also on the November 3 ballot in California and contain competing measure provisions that would nullify Proposition 40 if all the measures are approved but Propositions 41 and 42 receive more votes than Proposition 40. Proposition 40 also contains a competing measure provision that would nullify Propositions 41 and 42 if Proposition 40 receives more votes. 

### How would net worth be calculated?

*See also: [Measure design](#Measure_design)*

To determine an individual's net worth, the initiative would account for the following assets:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   publicly traded securities at their market value on December 31, 2026;
*   private business interests;
*   assets under a sole proprietorship;
*   grantor trusts;
*   art, collectibles, intellectual property, vehicles, other financial instruments not publicly traded, and debts or liabilities owed to the individual ($5 million exclusion of total combined asset value from net worth);
*   Roth IRA or other Roth-type retirement accounts valued above $10 million;
*   property valued at more than $1 million transferred after October 15, 2025, for less than fair market value; and
*   dependent's assets in excess of $50,000.

Real estate and pensions would be excluded from the calculation of net worth.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

*See also: [Wealth tax ballot measures](#Wealth_tax_ballot_measures) and [Ballot measures related to income and wealth taxes, 2026](/Ballot_measures_related_to_income_and_wealth_taxes,_2026 "Ballot measures related to income and wealth taxes, 2026")*

The California wealth tax initiative would be the first ballot measure in the country to enact such a tax. Additionally, in 2026, there are nine statewide ballot measures in six states related to income and wealth tax policy. Of these measures, two would allow, create, or increase income taxes; five would prohibit, cap, or decrease income taxes; one would allow, create, or increase wealth taxes; and one would prohibit, cap, or decrease wealth taxes.

## Measure design

*See also: [Text of measure](#Text_of_measure)*

**Click on the following sections** for summaries of the different provisions of the ballot measure. 

Expand All

Wealth tax on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion

The initiative would levy a one-time tax of 5% on taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion, including shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest. A married couple would be considered one individual. The tax would be retroactive and apply to any taxpayer residing in the state as of January 1, 2026. For individuals with net worth between $1 billion and $1.1 billion, the tax rate would be reduced by 0.1% (but not below 0%) for each $2 million their net worth falls below $1.1 billion. The tax would be due with an individual's 2027 tax filings.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 

The initiative would allow individuals to pay the tax in five equal installments beginning in 2027, with each subsequent payment subject to an annual deferral charge of 7.5% of the remaining unpaid balance.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

Net worth calculation

To determine an individual's net worth, the initiative would account for the following assets:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

*   publicly traded securities at their market value on December 31, 2026;
*   private business interests;
*   assets under a sole proprietorship;
*   grantor trusts;
*   art, collectibles, intellectual property, vehicles, other financial instruments not publicly traded, and debts or liabilities owed to the individual ($5 million exclusion of total combined asset value from net worth);
*   Roth IRA or other Roth-type retirement accounts valued above $10 million;
*   property valued at more than $1 million transferred after October 15, 2025, for less than fair market value; and
*   dependent's assets in excess of $50,000.

Real estate and pensions would be excluded from the calculation of net worth.[\[7\]](#cite_note-lao-7) 

The initiative would account for the following debts as reductions to an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   recourse debts for which the individual is personally liable;
*   nonrecourse debts up to the value of the collateral securing them; and
*   debts and other liabilities resulting from a sole proprietorship but not from a partnership, limited liability company, or other business entity.

The following debts or liabilities would not lower an individual's net worth:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*   related-party debts;
*   charitable pledges made after October 15, 2025; and
*   contingent liabilities with outcomes uncertain within five years.

Revenue allocation

The initiative would create the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, where all taxes, interest, and penalties resulting from the initiative would be deposited. The fund would have two sub-accounts: the Billionaire Tax Health account, where 90% of the revenue would be deposited, and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account with the remaining 10% of revenue. The initiative would require the health account to fund Medi-Cal and other health coverage programs for low- and moderate-income individuals, as well as health care access, benefits, and services. The initiative would require revenue in the education account to fund public education from K-14, reductions in federal or state appropriations, and reductions in food assistance programs such as CalFresh, CalFAP, CalFood, or California's Universal Meals Program for school meals.[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1)

  
 

The initiative contains a provision that would exclude the revenue generated by the tax from the state’s General Fund when calculating the state minimum guarantee for education funding, which was enacted by [Proposition 98](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)") in 1988.

The ballot measure would amend [Section 37 of Article XIII](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution#Section_37 "Article XIII, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution"). The following underlined text would be added:[\[1\]](#cite_note-text-1) 

*Note*: Hover over the text and scroll to see the full text. 

Sec. 37. 

(a) This Section authorizes and enables a one-time tax on the accumulated wealth of California billionaires, imposed on those individuals who are California residents within the meaning of Sections 17014 and 17015.5 of the Revenue and Taxation Code as of the tax obligation date as defined in the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act. 

(b) The following definitions apply to this Section: 

(1) "Act" refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act. 

(2) "Reserve Fund" refers to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, created by this Act. 

(c) Notwithstanding any other provision of the Constitution, the Act provides for taxation on all forms of personal property and wealth, whether tangible or intangible, and allows for the classification of personal property and wealth for differential taxation or for exemption, for the purpose of imposing the one-time tax on the wealth of California billionaires. Personal property and wealth that is so taxed includes, but is not limited to, shares of capital stock, bonds or other evidences of indebtedness, and any legal or equitable interest therein. 

(d) The 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund is hereby created in the State Treasury. All revenues from the Act—including taxes, interest, and penalties, and less refunds—shall be deposited in the State Treasury by the State Controller to the credit of the Reserve Fund. After accounting for administrative expenses as provided by law, the Controller shall allocate and transfer the remaining moneys in the Reserve Fund to the following sub-accounts, which are hereby created: 90% to the Billionaire Tax Health Account and 10% to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account. The moneys in the Billionaire Tax Health Account and the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account shall be allocated as provided by law. 

(e) Notwithstanding any other law, the Reserve Fund is a special fund, permanently separate and apart from the General Fund or any other state fund or account. The taxes and the moneys resulting from the Act shall not be considered to be part of the General Fund, as that term is used in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 16300) of Part 2 of Division 4 of Title 2 of the Government Code; and shall not be considered "General Fund revenues," "state revenues," "moneys," or "proceeds of taxes" under Section 8 of Article XIIIB for the purposes of any section of Article XIIIB, or Sections 8 or 8.5 of Article XVI. Any revenue raised through the Act shall also not be considered "personal income taxes paid on net capital gains" for purposes of Section 20 of Article XVI. The taxes levied by this Act are not "ad valorem taxes on real property" for purposes of Section 1 of Article XIIIA. To the extent any provision of Article XIIIA would otherwise be construed to limit, restrict, or apply to the rate, base, valuation, or imposition of the tax authorized by this Section, that provision shall not apply to, and is superseded by, this Section. Notwithstanding Section 16305.7 of the Government Code, any interest or dividends earned on moneys in the Reserve Fund shall be retained in the Reserve Fund and used solely for the specific purposes set forth in this subdivision and as provided by the Act. 

(f) "Appropriations subject to limitation" of each entity of government and the state under Article XIIIB shall not include appropriations of revenue from the Reserve Fund. No adjustment in the appropriations limit of any entity of government shall be required pursuant to Section 3 of Article XIIIB as a result of revenue being deposited in or appropriated from the Reserve Fund. 

(g) Except as provided in Sections 16310 and 16381 of the Government Code as those sections read on January 1, 2025, and except as otherwise provided in this Act, moneys in the Reserve Fund shall not be borrowed, loaned, or otherwise transferred to the General Fund or any other state or local fund or account. Moneys deposited into the Reserve Fund shall only be used for the specific purposes provided by law. Action shall not be taken that permanently or temporarily changes the status of the Reserve Fund or borrows, diverts, or appropriates the moneys in the Reserve Fund in a manner inconsistent with this subdivision. 

(h) Notwithstanding Section 32 or any other provision of law, a facial challenge to the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act is authorized to be adjudicated through a validation action under Chapter 6 of Part 27 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, Section 50314 without requiring the payment of the tax claimed to be facially invalid. This subdivision is adopted without implication as to current authority or the development of law other than this Act. Nothing in this subdivision limits any taxpayer's right to pay a tax imposed under this Act and seek a refund or judicial review, or to bring any other action that is otherwise authorized by law and not inconsistent with this subdivision.[\[8\]](#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-8)

Real estate, most pensions, and retirement accounts (with some caps) are generally excluded. Revenue (estimated in the tens of billions, though highly uncertain) would primarily fund health care (90%), with the rest for education, food assistance, and administration. It is structured as both a constitutional amendment and statute, with provisions attempting to exempt it from certain existing California spending limits.[[1]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/title-summary.htm)

The measure’s design—particularly the **retroactive residency snapshot** (January 1, 2026, well before the November 3, 2026 vote) combined with **100% default apportionment of worldwide wealth** to California—has drawn extensive criticism for potential constitutional defects. If enacted, it would almost certainly face immediate, extensive litigation. Below is a summary of the primary arguments, focusing on the Commerce Clause and retroactivity as requested.

### Dormant Commerce Clause Challenges
The U.S. Constitution’s Commerce Clause (and its dormant implication) limits state taxes that unduly burden interstate (or foreign) commerce. Courts apply the four-prong *Complete Auto Transit, Inc. v. Brady* (1977) test: (1) substantial nexus with the taxing state; (2) fair apportionment; (3) no discrimination against interstate commerce; and (4) a fair relationship to services provided by the state.

Critics argue Proposition 40 fails all or most prongs:
- **Nexus and apportionment**: It uses a single-day residency snapshot to tax 100% of a taxpayer’s *worldwide* net worth by default, including assets created, held, or located entirely outside California, and even post-departure appreciation for those who leave during 2026. This lacks a sufficient connection to California for out-of-state wealth and is not fairly apportioned (it risks multiple taxation of the same assets). Alternative apportionment is available but requires taxpayers to prove by “clear and convincing evidence” that the default is “grossly disproportionate.”[[2]](https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/why-californias-wealth-tax-wont-survive)
- **Discrimination and relatedness**: It treats in-state and out-of-state wealth identically without distinction, which can constitute discrimination against interstate commerce. Taxing full worldwide wealth based on one day’s residency bears little relation to California services provided. Similar issues arise under the Foreign Commerce Clause due to risks of international double taxation.[[3]](https://www.bakerbotts.com/thought-leadership/publications/2026/june/the-california-billionaire-tax-act-constitutional-limits-on-implementation)

The measure’s own text acknowledges potential invalidity of its apportionment formula and includes a broad severability/reformation clause instructing courts to adjust dates or provisions rather than strike the whole law. Defenders (including some of the measure’s academic architects) counter that it is non-discriminatory, applies equally regardless of where assets are located, and provides credits for similar taxes paid to other states, so there is “no serious argument” of a Commerce Clause violation.[[4]](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/galle-gamage-shanskeCBTAlegal.pdf)

Courts have historically been reluctant to “reform” Commerce Clause-violating tax statutes, often striking them instead.

### Retroactivity and Due Process
The January 1, 2026 residency date (and December 31 valuation) makes the tax retroactive by roughly 10–11 months if voters approve it in November. Retroactive tax changes are not automatically unconstitutional, but they face Due Process scrutiny under the 14th Amendment.

- **Critics’ view**: This is a “wholly new tax” (not a mere rate adjustment or correction to an existing tax), applied to completed events and people who may have already left the state. Supreme Court precedents like *Blodgett v. Holden* (1927) and *Untermyer v. Anderson* (1928) struck down retroactive application of a new gift tax. Later cases like *United States v. Carlton* (1994) distinguished those as involving a “wholly new tax” and upheld more modest retroactivity for existing taxes under rational-basis review, but did not overrule the earlier distinction. The snapshot also creates due process problems by taxing wealth accumulated after departure or with no California connection, and by using presumptive valuations (e.g., for private companies) that may be hard to rebut. It may also burden the right to travel.[[5]](https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/state/california-billionaire-wealth-tax-legal-challenges/)
- **Defenders’ view**: Retroactivity to the start of the calendar year is routine for tax legislation (including the original 1913 federal income tax and many California measures). It is not a “wholly new tax” because California already taxes forms of wealth (property taxes, vehicle taxes). Analogous to *Welch v. Henry* (1938), it taxes an involuntary status (being a billionaire) in an emergency context (federal health care funding cuts). Courts have not struck down a tax as unconstitutionally retroactive since 1928, and *Carlton* applies a deferential standard. The measure relies on existing valuation and residency rules.[[6]](https://scocablog.com/the-retroactivity-provision-in-proposition-40/)

A court could potentially reform the dates (as the measure invites) to make it prospective, but because it is designed as a *one-time* tax, invalidating the retroactive elements could gut much of its intended effect.

- **Takings Clause**: Critics call the 5% levy confiscatory (especially with illiquid assets and forced sales); defenders note that taxes are generally not “takings.”
- **Bills of Attainder**: Targeting a small, identifiable group (~200 billionaires) with punitive intent.
- **Due process for trusts and valuations**: Insufficient minimum contacts for some trusts (*Kaestner* precedent) and burdensome rebuttal standards for private asset values.
- State constitutional issues (e.g., interaction with Proposition 13 or spending limits, though the measure tries to exempt itself).

The Legislative Analyst’s Office has noted revenue uncertainty due to behavioral responses (billionaire flight) and litigation. Competing measures (Props 41 and 42) could also nullify it if they receive more votes.

**Outlook**: Legal experts on both sides agree litigation would be immediate and prolonged. Critics (Tax Foundation, Hoover Institution analyses, law firms like Baker Botts) view the defects as fatal or severely limiting. Defenders argue the challenges are overstated and rest on outdated or inapplicable precedents. Outcomes would depend on how courts apply *Complete Auto*, the “wholly new tax” distinction, and the measure’s severability language. No U.S. state currently has a broad wealth tax of this type, so this would be a novel test case.","citations":["https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/40/title-summary.htm","https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/why-californias-wealth-tax-wont-survive","https://www.bakerbotts.com/thought-leadership/publications/2026/june/the-california-billionaire-tax-act-constitutional-limits-on-implementation","https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/galle-gamage-shanskeCBTAlegal.pdf","https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/state/california-billionaire-wealth-tax-legal-challenges/","https://scocablog.com/the-retroactivity-provision-in-proposition-40/"],"allowed_domains":null}

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"wealth tax evidence France Norway Spain Switzerland capital flight academic review Saez Zucman","content":"**Academic evidence on wealth taxes in France, Norway, Spain, and Switzerland shows significant behavioral responses—including some capital flight, migration, avoidance, and evasion—but these are often modest in aggregate economic terms, highly dependent on tax design (exemptions, enforcement, residency-based taxation), and smaller than intensive-margin effects like reduced saving or reporting.** Revenues have typically been low relative to theoretical potential due to narrow bases. Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman (2022) review the European experience, arguing that past taxes failed due to political choices (exemptions for business assets/homes, weak enforcement, tax competition via residency rules) rather than inherent economic impossibility; they advocate a broad-base tax with strong information reporting and measures against expatriation.[[1]](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pandp.20221055)

### France (ISF wealth tax, 1980s–2018; replaced by real-estate-only IFI)
The ISF had a narrow base due to exemptions (especially owner-manager business equity) and a tax ceiling (wealth + income tax capped at 75% of taxable income). Saez and Zucman note that in 2016 it raised only ~0.2% of GDP versus a theoretical ~0.8% from a 1% tax on the top 1%; for the very top, exemptions reduced the effective rate dramatically (e.g., from 1.5% to ~0.15% for the top 0.001%). Bach et al. (matching tax and business data) confirm this concentrated at the top.[[2]](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/SZ2022AEA.pdf)

Capital flight estimates vary: French government figures cited ~10,000 people with €35 billion in assets leaving 2000–2015; economist Éric Pichet estimated ~€200 billion in capital flight 1988–2007, with possible GDP growth drag of ~0.2%. After 2018 repeal, some reversal occurred (net inflows of former ISF payers). A Conseil d’analyse économique (CAE) study found low mobility among the top 1% of capital-income earners (~0.2% annual emigration, below the national average) and negligible aggregate effects (e.g., a reform raising €4 billion would cut employment/value-added by at most 0.04–0.05%). Garbinti et al. document evasion responses to reduced reporting requirements (reported wealth growth ~20% lower). Zucman has noted that even mass billionaire flight would have tiny revenue impact (~0.03% of GDP).[[3]](https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/failures-wealth-taxation)

### Norway (ongoing wealth tax; rate hikes in 2022)
Norway taxes a relatively broad share of households (~13% liable). Recent 2022 increases (top rate to 1.1%, plus other capital tax changes) prompted high-profile emigrations (e.g., >30 billionaires/multimillionaires in 2022, more than the prior 13 years combined; Ministry of Finance estimated ~$15 billion in deferred income taken abroad in 2022–2023). Some studies highlight avoidance (shifting to closely held firms with valuation discounts).

Scandinavian evidence (Jakobsen, Kleven, Kolsrud, Landais, Muñoz; using Sweden/Denmark reforms, relevant analog) finds a 1 percentage point (pp) rise in the top wealth tax rate reduces the stock of wealthy taxpayers by ~2% (semi-elasticity of out-migration ~-0.17). Businesses of emigrating owners see large drops (employment -33%, value-added -34%), but reallocation mitigates this. Aggregate effects of a 1pp hike are modest: employment -0.02%, investment -0.07%, value-added -0.10%. Migration-related revenue loss is ~$0.22 per dollar raised (vs. $0.54 from intensive-margin responses like saving/avoidance). A Norway-specific analysis of 2021–2024 reforms estimated at most 74–98 extra emigrations (~1.78% of top 0.1%), with wealth-tax revenues still rising substantially and no clear investment drop. Critics of larger GDP-loss claims (e.g., 1.3%) argue they over-extrapolate from non-representative samples.[[4]](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20241596)

### Spain (ongoing, decentralized wealth tax)
Spain’s tax (reintroduced post-2011, with regional variation) has a narrow base and high combined rates with other capital taxes. Madrid’s zero rate created an internal “tax haven.” Agrawal, Foremny, and Martínez-Toledano find that 5–6 years after reintroduction, Madrid’s stock of wealthy individuals rose 7.5–10% relative to other regions (elasticity similar to income-tax mobility estimates); smaller inter-regional differentials had little effect. Evasion appears dominant over pure migration in models. Mobility caused income-tax revenue losses ~6 times larger than direct wealth-tax losses; Spain forgoes ~5% of wealth-tax revenue nationally, with Madrid gaining at others’ expense and exacerbating regional inequality. A 2022 national “solidarity” backstop overrode some regional credits.[[5]](https://diposit.ub.edu/bitstreams/de947c26-299d-491a-aead-5315eefb84b8/download)

### Switzerland (ongoing cantonal wealth taxes)
Switzerland has the broadest coverage (~25% of households) and highest revenue share among these countries (~1% of GDP, 3–4% of tax revenue), with rates varying by canton (typically 0.2–0.5%). Brülhart, Gruber, Krapf, and Schmidheiny (using cantonal variation) find high responsiveness: a 1pp drop in the wealth tax raises reported taxable wealth by ≥43% after 6 years (or a 0.1pp increase lowers it by 3.5%). Decomposition (from quasi-random reforms): ~24% taxpayer mobility, ~21% housing-price capitalization, remainder mostly evasion (no third-party reporting of financial wealth; savings explain little). Bunching below thresholds occurs. Switzerland’s success relative to others is attributed to lower rates, broader base, and federal constraints preventing zero rates.[[6]](https://doi.org/10.1257/pol.20200258)

### Overall Academic Consensus and Saez-Zucman Perspective
Intensive-margin responses (avoidance, evasion, portfolio shifts, reduced accumulation) typically dominate extensive-margin ones (migration/capital flight). Elasticities are large for reported wealth in low-enforcement settings (Switzerland) but aggregate GDP/employment effects remain small even when wealthy entrepreneurs leave, due to reallocation. Design is critical: exemptions (business assets, homes) and self-reporting eroded bases; residency-based taxation enabled flight (unlike U.S. citizenship-based rules). Post-CRS automatic information exchange has reduced some offshore evasion.

Saez and Zucman emphasize that European taxes were not “true” comprehensive wealth taxes and that better 21st-century design (broad market-value base, few exemptions, third-party reporting, exit taxes or continued taxation of expatriates, possibly EU-wide coordination) could succeed. They contrast this with U.S. proposals. Critics (e.g., Tax Foundation, Cato) highlight repeated repeals due to flight, low revenue, and administrative costs, arguing even remaining taxes show the same issues. Recent Norway/Spain episodes and Swiss elasticities illustrate ongoing challenges, but rigorous papers generally find effects too small to make well-designed taxes self-defeating. Evidence predates some modern enforcement tools, so extrapolation requires caution.","citations":["https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pandp.20221055","https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/SZ2022AEA.pdf","https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/failures-wealth-taxation","https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20241596","https://diposit.ub.edu/bitstreams/de947c26-299d-491a-aead-5315eefb84b8/download","https://doi.org/10.1257/pol.20200258"],"allowed_domains":null}

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"Saez Zucman response California billionaire tax flight Rauh revenue estimate 2026","content":"**Saez, Zucman, and co-author Jasper Boll estimate that California’s proposed one-time 5% billionaire wealth tax (Proposition 40, on the November 2026 ballot) could raise about $100 billion, with comparatively minor income-tax losses from any mobility.** They argue Rauh’s much lower (or negative) net-revenue figures rest on overly pessimistic assumptions about tax flight, residency changes, and income-tax payments by the ultra-wealthy.[[1]](https://www.vpm.org/npr-story/two-economists-studied-californias-billionaire-tax-they-reached-wildly-different-conclusions/)

Boll, Saez, and Zucman (NBER WP 35218, revised August 2026) put California billionaire wealth at ~$2.3 trillion by mid-2026 (up 144% from 2023–2025, driven by the AI boom). A 5% levy on that, reduced 10% for avoidance/evasion/some pre-cutoff departures, yields their ~$100 billion benchmark. They also present scenarios with more aggressive leavers (~$84–89 billion) or additional “missing” billionaires not on Forbes lists (higher figures). They note billionaires currently pay only ~0.2% of wealth (~$3.2 billion/year) in California income tax—about 2.4% of the state’s income-tax revenue—and even less relative to their wealth gains (1.6% of 2019–2025 gains). For the top 4 (Page, Brin, Zuckerberg, Huang), SEC data show even lower California income-tax payments on company wealth (~0.04–0.07% of wealth). Thus, even if some leave, lost future income taxes would be small relative to the one-time haul. A permanent annual wealth tax, they add, could still raise substantial net revenue after mobility.[[2]](https://taxobservatory.world/publication/california-billionaires-wealth-taxes-and-wealth-tax-revenue-estimates/)

**Their main critiques of Rauh/Jaros (and related Hoover/NBER work estimating ~$30–40 billion collected but a mean NPV of –$39 billion after exits, litigation risk, and lost income taxes):**
- **Residency/tax flight before the cutoff is overstated.** Rauh identifies 7 high-profile billionaires (Larry Page, Sergey Brin, Peter Thiel, Don Hankey, Steven Spielberg, Travis Kalanick, David Sacks) as having left, removing ~30% of the tax base (~$30 billion in potential revenue). Saez/Zucman dispute that these (or others) successfully ended California tax residency in the short window. Changing residency requires more than a move (e.g., schools, burial plots, professional/social ties); legal experts they cite view last-minute changes as unlikely to hold. Brin, for example, still commutes to Silicon Valley work. They treat some as remaining residents and include an “aggressive-leaver” scenario that still shows high revenue. They argue it is “almost impossible” to sever ties before January 1, 2026.[[1]](https://www.vpm.org/npr-story/two-economists-studied-californias-billionaire-tax-they-reached-wildly-different-conclusions/)
- **Permanent-exit assumption is inconsistent.** Why leave forever over a one-time tax owed based on 2026 residency? It would only make sense if expecting the tax to become annual/permanent (as some proponents, including Saez, have discussed as a possible future step). But Rauh scores only the one-time tax while assuming infinite lost income-tax streams from leavers—without counting extra revenue from any future annual tax (a 1% annual tax would raise far more in present-value terms). Zucman has called the Rauh analysis “spectacularly misleading” on this and related points.[[3]](https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988817431126153)
- **Income-tax payments by leavers (especially the top few) are overstated.** Rauh’s team estimates California billionaires pay $3.3–5.8 billion/year in state income tax. Saez/Zucman say their own figures are similar in aggregate (~$3.2–4.3 billion), but Rauh overstates payments by the key leavers (top 3 or so) by a factor of ~5 relative to SEC filings on compensation, dividends, stock sales, etc. (e.g., Page and Brin had years with $0 California income tax on Alphabet wealth despite huge unrealized gains). If they leave, California loses little income tax. They also note Rauh’s higher income-tax assumptions for the very top.[[4]](https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/saez-tpe26-presentation.pdf)
- Other points: The 10% haircut already builds in some avoidance. Litigation/constitutional risks exist but are not assumed to wipe out most revenue. Broader economic dynamism/job effects are acknowledged as a concern but not the focus of their scoring. They have a real-time wealth tracker and emphasize the tax is small relative to recent wealth gains yet large relative to current taxes paid.[[5]](https://saez-zucman-audit-replication.vercel.app/p/boll-saez-zucman-2026-california-billionaires.html)

Rauh has replied that documented public departures occurred, sophisticated taxpayers/lawyers can establish residency, statements by proponents (including Saez/Zucman) about a “global movement” or possible permanence give rational reason to leave, income-tax estimates are close in aggregate, and the one-time framing does not prevent scoring behavioral responses or future losses. The Legislative Analyst’s Office has given a more cautious “tens of billions” range. Voters decide November 3, 2026.[[6]](https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/golden-state-or-golden-exit)

Primary sources include Boll/Saez/Zucman NBER WP 35218 and related presentations; Rauh/Jaros NBER work and Substack; and contemporaneous coverage of the exchange.","citations":["https://www.vpm.org/npr-story/two-economists-studied-californias-billionaire-tax-they-reached-wildly-different-conclusions/","https://taxobservatory.world/publication/california-billionaires-wealth-taxes-and-wealth-tax-revenue-estimates/","https://x.com/gabriel_zucman/status/2112988817431126153","https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/saez-tpe26-presentation.pdf","https://saez-zucman-audit-replication.vercel.app/p/boll-saez-zucman-2026-california-billionaires.html","https://fiscalrealitycheck.substack.com/p/golden-state-or-golden-exit"],"allowed_domains":null}

The measure includes "no supplant" language, but opponents argue loopholes could allow replacement of existing funds.[[2]](https://ballotexplained.com/measures/california/proposition-40)

If these revenues instead flowed into the General Fund, Prop 98 would automatically allocate ~40% to schools and community colleges. There is a legitimate debate to be had about whether the wealthiest Californians should pay more in taxes. But Proposition 40 is the wrong tax, structured the wrong way, and would only make California’s budget problems worse.

Even voters who believe billionaires should contribute more should reject a measure that is so poorly drafted. Proposition 40 is ballot-box budgeting at its worst: a one-time tax that would raise tens of billions of dollars ostensibly for healthcare — but has insufficient guardrails to ensure the funds are spent to actually address Californians’ most pressing healthcare needs.

Instead, the funds could go to any interest group, including health insurance companies, pharmaceutical companies and for-profit hospitals. These sectors all play an important role in our healthcare system, but we should not allocate precious taxpayer dollars to subsidize these for-profit corporations.

Equally problematic: Proposition 40’s proponents excluded other key state priorities like education, public safety, housing, wildfire prevention and more. California is confronting persistent deficits, struggling public schools, a housing and homelessness crisis, rising costs for families, and growing demands for wildfire prevention, public safety and other essential services. Yet Proposition 40 provides little to nothing for these priorities.

Supporters describe Proposition 40 as a one-time solution to an immediate crisis. Californians have heard that before. Proposition 30 was sold as [a temporary tax increase](https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx) in 2012. Voters [later extended](https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016) much of it through 2030. Once government programs become dependent on a revenue source, “temporary” taxes have a way of becoming permanent political expectations.

The reality is that one-time taxes create a fiscal cliff, which leads to new and additional taxes when the money runs out. Even worse, this measure would drive out some of our state’s most successful residents, taking jobs, economic benefits and billions in tax revenue with them.

And Proposition 40 would establish an especially dangerous precedent. If one interest group can write a tax measure, target a politically unpopular group and dedicate the proceeds to its preferred programs, others will follow.

That is no way to govern a state with an economy larger than most countries.

California can ask the wealthy to contribute more without embracing a measure this flawed. Proposition 40 is a temporary tax masquerading as a fiscal solution, a permanent precedent for ballot-box budgeting and the wrong answer to the very real problems facing California.

Vote no on Proposition 40.

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"pdftotext prop40-text OR "2026 Billionaire Tax Act" section 3 purposes valuation 7.5 apportionment","content":"**Proposition 40 (the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act)** is a California ballot initiative (Initiative 25-0024A1) that would impose a one-time 5% tax on the worldwide net worth of certain California-resident billionaires (residency locked as of January 1, 2026; valuation as of December 31, 2026). Revenues would go primarily to health care (90%), with the rest to education and food assistance. The full official text is available from the California Attorney General.[[1]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

### Section 3: Purpose and Intent
The Act’s stated purposes are:

(a) The purpose of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, referred to herein as the “Act,” is to protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs, by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth.

(b) Revenues from the Act are intended to respond to urgent, existing health care, education, and nutrition needs that are being worsened by reductions in federal and state funding and by broader fiscal uncertainty facing the state.

(c) By designating billionaire wealth the source of this critical revenue, the Act confronts the fundamental unfairness that arises because a large percentage of billionaire wealth is never taxed by the State due to billionaires’ unique ability to control the timing, location, and amount of income tax that they pay.

(d) The Act raises funding for health care, education, and food assistance by imposing a narrowly applicable, one-time tax that is administratively feasible and efficient to enforce against all billionaires in the State.

(e) The Act is intended to treat similarly situated taxpayers and assets similarly, except to the extent that sound tax policy requires otherwise.[[1]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

### Valuation Rules (Including the 7.5 Multiplier)
Valuation of net worth generally uses fair market value, with specific rules in proposed Revenue and Taxation Code § 50303. Publicly traded assets use market trading value on the valuation date. Directly held real property (or via revocable trust) is excluded.

For private business interests (equity, ownership, debt, or other interests, except sole proprietorships and publicly traded assets):

- Taxpayers report ownership percentage, GAAP book value at year-end, and book profits.
- For voting/control rights: ownership percentage is presumed not less than the taxpayer’s share of overall voting or direct control rights.
- For profits interests: ownership percentage is presumed not less than the maximum profits percentage the taxpayer may earn (even if subject to unmet conditions).
- Default formula (presumed fair market value): **(entity GAAP book value at year-end + 7.5 × average GAAP book profits over the current tax year and preceding two years, if available) × taxpayer’s ownership percentage**. Losses are treated as zero (not negative). For private equity entities, this cannot be less than the sum of values of owned entities minus certain liabilities. Alternative accounting methods may be allowed if consistently used.
- This presumption can be overridden by a certified appraisal (by taxpayer or Franchise Tax Board) showing by clear and convincing evidence that it substantially overstates or understates actual value. Appraisers face potential penalties (up to 4% of understatement). No minority, lack-of-marketability, or similar discounts that would reduce a partial interest below pro-rata value of the whole asset.[[1]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

There is also a **7.5% annual nondeductible deferral charge** on unpaid balances if the tax is paid in five equal annual installments (instead of in full with the 2026 return).[[1]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

### Apportionment
Proposed § 50306 provides:

- **Standard apportionment**: 100% of the tax is apportioned to California for applicable individuals and trusts, without reduction or multiplier based on residency history (residency determined as of the January 1, 2026 tax obligation date). This supersedes other rules, including part-year residence.

- **Alternative apportionment**: Available via petition (or FTB requirement) if the standard method does not fairly represent the extent to which the taxpayer’s excessive wealth was accumulated in or substantially sustained by California. The petitioner must prove by clear and convincing evidence that (A) the wealth did not substantially accumulate in California **and** (B) it was not substantially sustained in California for at least 365 days in the aggregate during the 48-month period ending on the valuation date. Alternatively, it can be shown that the U.S. or California Constitution or federal law prohibits the standard method.

  Relief generally cannot reduce the California percentage below 25%, unless a court/OTA finds a lower (or zero) percentage is required to avoid grossly disproportionate taxation. The Board may issue regulations with examples. If residency-based apportionment is held invalid, fallback to standard personal income tax residency rules applies. Credits are available for certain taxes paid to other jurisdictions.[[1]](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0024A1%20%28Billionaire%20Tax%20%29.pdf)

These provisions are designed to be administrable for a small number of taxpayers (~200–250 billionaires) while addressing potential constitutional issues (e.g., Commerce Clause apportionment). The measure includes severability, anti-avoidance rules, and expedited judicial review. Competing ballot measures (Props 41/42) could affect it if they receive more votes.
